story_ideas.title: Tracking Implementation of the 2025 Reconciliation Law: Medicaid Work Requirements Data and Policies
story_ideas.headline: Your state has picked how it will make you prove you qualify for Medicaid
story_ideas.angle: A state-by-state read of the work requirements tracker published 09/09/26, written for the adult child who handles a parent's Medicaid paperwork.
story_ideas.hook: The tracker went live on 09/09/26 with state and national policy data and no monitored publisher has matched it.
story_ideas.summary: Detailed state and national data related to the 2025 Reconciliation Law Medicaid Work Requirements
story_ideas.consumer: Look up your state in the tracker and find out what documentation it expects, how often, and what an exemption looks like before a renewal notice arrives.
story_ideas.b2b: Providers serving dual-eligible and Medicaid long-term care residents can read the tracker as a forecast of which states will generate the most eligibility churn, and staff their billing offices accordingly.
story_ideas.chart: The figures in the finding are the spine of a simple graphic.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: A family that does not know its state's documentation rule can lose coverage for someone who still qualifies.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap and the tracker breaks to the state level, so it localizes cleanly and supports a comparison chart.

story_ideas.title: Prior Authorization Metrics Provide New Insights into Insurer Practices, but Gaps Remain
story_ideas.headline: At least one in eight prior authorization requests was turned down last year
story_ideas.angle: A plain-language walk through the 2025 prior authorization figures for Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care and the federally facilitated ACA Marketplaces, for anyone whose plan requires approval before care.
story_ideas.hook: The analysis puts a number on denials across three markets and says outright that the data has limits.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask your plan whether the service you need requires prior authorization, get the denial in writing if it comes, and file the appeal rather than accepting the first answer.
story_ideas.b2b: Denial rates that vary widely by insurer are a contracting and revenue-cycle variable, not just a patient-experience problem.
story_ideas.why: Knowing a denial is common, appealable and documented is the difference between paying out of pocket and getting the service covered.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap; the insurer-level variation is the chartable part.

story_ideas.title: How States Align Postsecondary and Workforce Strategies
story_ideas.headline: The state plans that decide whether anyone is trained to care for you
story_ideas.angle: A read of all Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act plans across five plan cycles, aimed at readers who cannot find a home care aide.
story_ideas.hook: New this run and unmatched by monitored publishers: an analysis of every WIOA plan across five cycles, with benchmarks for coordination between postsecondary education and workforce systems.
story_ideas.summary: The authors analyze all Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act plans across five plan cycles, identifying strategies that policymakers can use to benchmark plans and strengthen coordination between postsecondary education and workforce systems.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are waiting on home care hours, your state's workforce plan is the document that says whether training pipelines for direct care are being built at all.
story_ideas.b2b: Operators can use the benchmarking framework to argue for direct care inclusion in the next state plan cycle rather than reacting to it after adoption.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: Families competing for scarce aides gain from knowing where training capacity is decided, and where their state has left direct care out.
story_ideas.note: Not aging-specific on its face, which is why the aging trades have not run it; the direct care read is the differentiator.

story_ideas.title: Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services for Older Adults: A Primer
story_ideas.headline: The Medicaid benefit that keeps you home, and the reasons you may not get it
story_ideas.angle: A primer-driven piece on HCBS access gaps for older adults with disabilities, for anyone weighing home care against a facility.
story_ideas.hook: The primer names the policy gaps that limit access to services designed to keep people out of institutions.
story_ideas.consumer: Find out whether your state's HCBS program has a waiting list and what the eligibility path is before a hospital discharge forces the decision.
story_ideas.b2b: Every HCBS access gap is a referral that lands in skilled nursing instead, which is a census and case-mix question for operators.
story_ideas.why: The difference between HCBS and a facility is where someone lives for the rest of their life.
story_ideas.note: Lightly covered; the state-level access comparison is where the original reporting sits.

story_ideas.title: Availability of Rural Hospitals Providing Inpatient Maternity Care in Medicaid
story_ideas.headline: The rural hospitals carrying Medicaid patients are the ones cutting service lines
story_ideas.angle: A rural access piece that starts from the maternity care analysis and asks what a service-line closure does to every other Medicaid patient at the same hospital.
story_ideas.hook: The data note maps which rural hospitals still provide inpatient maternity care to Medicaid enrollees and models what further closures would do.
story_ideas.consumer: If you live in a rural county, this is a way to see how thin your nearest hospital's service lines already are.
story_ideas.b2b: Rural hospital service-line economics determine whether post-acute and swing-bed capacity survives in the same building.
story_ideas.why: Rural residents who lose a hospital service line lose driving distance to care, not just one department.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap; the analysis is about maternity care, so the aging angle has to be reported rather than asserted.

story_ideas.title: Here's How Much Americans Rely on Social Security – at All Income Levels
story_ideas.headline: Social Security is doing more of the work than higher earners assume
story_ideas.angle: A reliance-by-income-level breakdown from the Center for Retirement Research release of 09/02/26, for readers building a retirement income plan.
story_ideas.hook: The finding cuts against the assumption that Social Security reliance is a low-income story.
story_ideas.consumer: Run your own numbers: what share of your expected retirement income is the benefit, and what happens to your budget if it is more than you thought.
story_ideas.b2b: Advisors and annuity writers are selling against a reliance profile that runs further up the income scale than their models assume.
story_ideas.why: Understating how much of your income the benefit carries produces a plan that fails at the first cost increase.
story_ideas.note: Lightly covered and national only; pair with a state cost-of-living cut for localization.

story_ideas.title: Social Security Ruling, SSR 26-2p; Titles II and XVI: Documenting and Evaluating Disability in Young Adults
story_ideas.headline: Social Security rewrote the disability rules for young adults, and aging parents are the ones who file
story_ideas.angle: What SSR 26-2p changes about documenting disability in young adults, written for the older parent managing an adult child's claim.
story_ideas.hook: The ruling published 09/01/26 rescinds and replaces SSR 11-2p and consolidates the documentation policy in one place.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are filing or appealing for an adult child, check the new ruling for what evidence the agency now expects before you submit.
story_ideas.b2b: Financial planners building special needs trusts and dual-generation plans have a new documentation standard to work against.
story_ideas.why: A claim assembled to the old standard can be denied on evidence grounds alone.
story_ideas.note: Lightly covered; the multigenerational planning angle is what makes it an aging story.

story_ideas.title: June 1-5 is Medicare Fraud Prevention Week. Here's How Americans Can Help Protect Themselves and Medicare.
story_ideas.headline: The Medicare statement in your mail is a fraud detector if you read it
story_ideas.angle: A how-to on catching billing fraud from your own Medicare paperwork, drawn from the federal agency's prevention guidance.
story_ideas.hook: The guidance puts the detection step in the beneficiary's hands rather than the plan's.
story_ideas.consumer: Compare every Medicare summary notice against the appointments you actually had, and report the lines that do not match.
story_ideas.b2b: Providers absorb the audit and chargeback consequences of billing patients never received.
story_ideas.why: Charges nobody checks become charges nobody recovers, and the beneficiary's number keeps getting used.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap, national, and evergreen enough to run against any billing cycle.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Fire Safety Deficiencies
story_ideas.headline: Three years of fire safety citations are posted for every nursing home
story_ideas.angle: A tour of the fire safety citation file, one citation per row with scope, severity and correction date, for the family touring a building this month.
story_ideas.hook: Fire safety citations sit in a separate file from health citations, so a facility can look clean on one and not the other.
story_ideas.consumer: Pull your facility's fire safety citations and ask the administrator which ones are still open and what the correction date was.
story_ideas.b2b: Life safety code citations follow a different survey track than health deficiencies, and open corrections are a compliance exposure operators can quantify.
story_ideas.why: A family reading only the health inspection record may never see the citation that matters most in a building at night.
story_ideas.note: Refreshed public file rather than an event; the story is the cut nobody makes, and it breaks to states and counties.

story_ideas.title: Medicaid Coverage for Women
story_ideas.headline: Medicaid's older enrollees are mostly women, and the program is built as if they were not
story_ideas.angle: A data-note read on how Medicaid currently serves women, focused on the years after 65 when coverage means long-term care.
story_ideas.hook: The data note assembles the current state of the program specifically as it affects women.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are a woman planning for long-term care, this is the coverage baseline you are planning against.
story_ideas.b2b: The resident population that Medicaid long-term care pays for skews female, which is a services and staffing design question.
story_ideas.why: Planning against a general Medicaid picture rather than the one that describes you produces the wrong estimate of what you will need to cover yourself.
story_ideas.note: Lightly covered; national only, so localization needs a state Medicaid enrollment overlay.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Medicaid coverage now survives or fails at two paperwork steps rather than one, and both records landed inside a month. KFF's Tracking Implementation of the 2025 Reconciliation Law: Medicaid Work Requirements Data and Policies published 09/09/26 with state and national data on what each state is asking enrollees to document, and no monitored publisher has matched it. KFF's prior authorization analysis, dated Aug 13, 2026, found insurers denied at least 1 in 8 standard prior authorization requests in 2025 across Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care and the federally facilitated ACA Marketplaces, with denial rates varying widely by insurer. One record covers getting in, the other covers getting care once you are in. The wider Medicare and Medicaid tag was the busiest beat this run, 26 items from 7 sources at 0.05 cohesion, and it is not one story; these two items are the thread inside it worth reporting, and Justice in Aging's Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services for Older Adults primer (08/20/26) is the third leg if the piece needs a long-term care spine.

**Why it matters:** For an older Medicaid enrollee or the family caregiver filing on their behalf, eligibility on paper is now two administrative tests away from an actual service. The prior authorization figure is the one hard number: at least one standard request in eight was denied in 2025, in the same three markets that carry Medicare Advantage enrollees and Medicaid managed care members. The work requirements tracker says what a state expects to be proved and how, which is what determines whether someone who qualifies stays enrolled. The KFF analysis itself notes the data's limitations, so the second finding of the story is what still cannot be looked up: denial reasons and outcomes by insurer, and documentation burden by state, are not published at a level a family can use.

**Why pitch this now:** The work requirements tracker went up 09/09/26 and is being updated as states stand the requirements up, so the state-by-state design table is current this month and will not be next. The prior authorization data covers 2025, the first full year against which the reconciliation law's coverage changes can be read.

**Angle:** Whether coverage that survives the 2025 reconciliation law on paper survives the documentation and authorization steps that come after it, and what the published data still will not tell an enrollee. Working title: "Covered on Paper." For payer and provider policy readers, and for the caregivers who file the forms.

- Two paperwork steps decide whether Medicaid coverage becomes care
- At least one in eight prior authorization requests was denied last year
- What your state wants you to prove to keep Medicaid

- **Fierce Healthcare** — its payer readers set the prior authorization thresholds this story counts, and its policy desk follows reconciliation law implementation state by state.
- **Modern Healthcare** — the denial rate across three markets is a business story for the plans and health systems absorbing the administrative cost.
- **Bankrate Retirement** — reaches the household deciding whether a parent's Medicaid coverage is worth the paperwork to keep, and pairs the coverage question with the cost of losing it.
- **SeniorLiving.org** — its audience is looking up eligibility rules before a move or a home care start, which is exactly where a state-by-state documentation table gets used.

- Hook: The primer names the policy gaps that limit access to services designed to keep people out of institutions.
- For readers: Find out whether your state's HCBS program has a waiting list and what the eligibility path is before a hospital discharge forces the decision.
- For the trade: Every HCBS access gap is a referral that lands in skilled nursing instead, which is a census and case-mix question for operators.
- Why it matters: The difference between HCBS and a facility is where someone lives for the rest of their life.
- Also: Lightly covered; the state-level access comparison is where the original reporting sits.
- Pitch to: Kiplinger, Skilled Nursing News

**The rural hospitals carrying Medicaid patients are the ones cutting service lines**
*Availability of Rural Hospitals Providing Inpatient Maternity Care in Medicaid*  
- Angle: A rural access piece that starts from the maternity care analysis and asks what a service-line closure does to every other Medicaid patient at the same hospital.
- Hook: The data note maps which rural hospitals still provide inpatient maternity care to Medicaid enrollees and models what further closures would do.
- For readers: If you live in a rural county, this is a way to see how thin your nearest hospital's service lines already are.
- For the trade: Rural hospital service-line economics determine whether post-acute and swing-bed capacity survives in the same building.
- Why it matters: Rural residents who lose a hospital service line lose driving distance to care, not just one department.
- Also: Confirmed gap; the analysis is about maternity care, so the aging angle has to be reported rather than asserted.
- Pitch to: Modern Healthcare, Fierce Healthcare

**Social Security is doing more of the work than higher earners assume**
*Here's How Much Americans Rely on Social Security – at All Income Levels*  
- Angle: A reliance-by-income-level breakdown from the Center for Retirement Research release of 09/02/26, for readers building a retirement income plan.
- Hook: The finding cuts against the assumption that Social Security reliance is a low-income story.
- For readers: Run your own numbers: what share of your expected retirement income is the benefit, and what happens to your budget if it is more than you thought.
- For the trade: Advisors and annuity writers are selling against a reliance profile that runs further up the income scale than their models assume.
- Why it matters: Understating how much of your income the benefit carries produces a plan that fails at the first cost increase.
- Also: Lightly covered and national only; pair with a state cost-of-living cut for localization.
- Pitch to: Bankrate Retirement, ThinkAdvisor

**Social Security rewrote the disability rules for young adults, and aging parents are the ones who file**
*Social Security Ruling, SSR 26-2p; Titles II and XVI: Documenting and Evaluating Disability in Young Adults*  
- Angle: What SSR 26-2p changes about documenting disability in young adults, written for the older parent managing an adult child's claim.
- Hook: The ruling published 09/01/26 rescinds and replaces SSR 11-2p and consolidates the documentation policy in one place.
- For readers: If you are filing or appealing for an adult child, check the new ruling for what evidence the agency now expects before you submit.
- For the trade: Financial planners building special needs trusts and dual-generation plans have a new documentation standard to work against.
- Why it matters: A claim assembled to the old standard can be denied on evidence grounds alone.
- Also: Lightly covered; the multigenerational planning angle is what makes it an aging story.
- Pitch to: GOBankingRates, Bankrate Retirement

**The Medicare statement in your mail is a fraud detector if you read it**
*June 1-5 is Medicare Fraud Prevention Week. Here's How Americans Can Help Protect Themselves and Medicare.*  
- Angle: A how-to on catching billing fraud from your own Medicare paperwork, drawn from the federal agency's prevention guidance.
- Hook: The guidance puts the detection step in the beneficiary's hands rather than the plan's.
- For readers: Compare every Medicare summary notice against the appointments you actually had, and report the lines that do not match.
- For the trade: Providers absorb the audit and chargeback consequences of billing patients never received.
- Why it matters: Charges nobody checks become charges nobody recovers, and the beneficiary's number keeps getting used.
- Also: Confirmed gap, national, and evergreen enough to run against any billing cycle.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Bankrate Retirement

**Three years of fire safety citations are posted for every nursing home**
*CMS refreshed dataset: Fire Safety Deficiencies*  
- Angle: A tour of the fire safety citation file, one citation per row with scope, severity and correction date, for the family touring a building this month.
- Hook: Fire safety citations sit in a separate file from health citations, so a facility can look clean on one and not the other.
- For readers: Pull your facility's fire safety citations and ask the administrator which ones are still open and what the correction date was.
- For the trade: Life safety code citations follow a different survey track than health deficiencies, and open corrections are a compliance exposure operators can quantify.
- Why it matters: A family reading only the health inspection record may never see the citation that matters most in a building at night.
- Also: Refreshed public file rather than an event; the story is the cut nobody makes, and it breaks to states and counties.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Long-Term Care News, Family Caregiver Alliance

**Medicaid's older enrollees are mostly women, and the program is built as if they were not**
*Medicaid Coverage for Women*  
- Angle: A data-note read on how Medicaid currently serves women, focused on the years after 65 when coverage means long-term care.
- Hook: The data note assembles the current state of the program specifically as it affects women.
- For readers: If you are a woman planning for long-term care, this is the coverage baseline you are planning against.
- For the trade: The resident population that Medicaid long-term care pays for skews female, which is a services and staffing design question.
- Why it matters: Planning against a general Medicaid picture rather than the one that describes you produces the wrong estimate of what you will need to cover yourself.
- Also: Lightly covered; national only, so localization needs a state Medicaid enrollment overlay.
- Pitch to: SeniorLiving.org, Modern Healthcare
